_commentaire: 16 fiches de Religious Studies GCE O Level (Cameroun), RÉDIGÉES par l'assistant, À RELIRE par un enseignant du GCE avant publication. Une session n'est citée que si une question de l'épreuve demandait cette méthode ou ce fait (seuil : 3 sessions ; 17 épreuves, années 2017-2026). Les fiches portent sur ce qui revient d'une session à l'autre (vocabulaire moral et social du Paper 1, méthodes de réponse, quelques sujets bibliques et islamiques du Paper 2), jamais sur des citations. Ton neutre. Plusieurs termes du Paper 1 dépendent de la convention du manuel (résidence, mariage, magie). Exercices « adapted from ».

notions.terme: What are the different types of love?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - friendship and love
notions.definition:
**Remember**:
- **Agape**: selfless, giving love that seeks the good of the other. Christians see it as the love of God.
- **Philia**: the love of friendship, without sexual attraction.
- **Storge**: natural affection in a family, for example between parents and children.
- **Eros** (erotic love): romantic love with sexual attraction.
- **Conjugal love**: the love between husband and wife.
- **Infatuation**: a strong, exciting attraction that is shallow and soon fades.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: A woman gives much of her time to care for sick strangers and expects nothing back. Which love is this?
Agape. She gives herself for the good of others, and they are neither her friends nor her family.
notions.piege: Do not choose agape just because a love is strong. A parent's natural affection is storge; a short, exciting passion is infatuation.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2026, Paper 1) Name the love (i) of a father for his daughter, (ii) between two good friends and (iii) directed to pleasure of the body.

notions.terme: What are the levels and types of conscience?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - conscience and moral choice
notions.definition:
**Remember**: conscience is a judgement of the mind (reason) that an act is right or wrong.
By time: **antecedent** (before the act), **concomitant** (during), **consequent** (after).
By type:
- **Certain**: sure of its judgement.
- **Doubtful**: cannot decide.
- **Erroneous**: judges wrongly, for example calls bad good.
- **Lax**: treats serious wrongs lightly.
- **Scrupulous**: very fearful; sees sin where there is none.
- **Perplexed**: sees wrong whichever choice is made.

A well-formed conscience helps a person to choose well and take responsibility.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: After lying to his mother, Tabi feels sorry and decides to tell the truth. Which level of conscience is at work?
Consequent conscience, because it judges the act after it has been done.
notions.piege: Erroneous and lax are not the same. An erroneous conscience is mistaken about right and wrong; a lax one is careless and excuses serious wrong.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2020, Paper 1) Name the conscience that judges an act (i) before, (ii) during and (iii) after it is done.
notions.reponse: (i) Antecedent conscience. (ii) Concomitant conscience. (iii) Consequent conscience.

notions.terme: What do the words for corruption and money crimes mean?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - corruption and embezzlement
notions.definition:
**Remember**:
- **Bribery**: giving or taking money or gifts to get an unfair favour.
- **Embezzlement**: taking for oneself money one was trusted to keep or manage.
- **Fraud**: deceiving people to gain something.
- **Forgery**: making or changing a document or signature to deceive.
- **Money laundering**: hiding the illegal source of money so that it looks clean.
- **Capital flight**: large sums leaving a country, for example stolen public funds sent abroad.
- **Nepotism**: unfair favour to relatives.
- **Tax evasion**: illegally avoiding tax.

In Cameroon, CONAC is the National Anti-Corruption Commission.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: A manager gives a job to his nephew although better candidates applied. Name this wrong and explain.
Nepotism. He favours a relative instead of choosing by merit, so the other candidates are treated unjustly.
notions.piege: Embezzlement is taking money that was in your care. Money laundering comes after a crime: it hides where the money came from.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2025, Paper 1) What is embezzlement? What name is given to copying and using another person's signature to deceive?
notions.reponse: Embezzlement is dishonestly taking for oneself money or property that one was trusted to keep or manage. Copying and using another person's signature to deceive is forgery.

notions.terme: What is a sect, a cult and a new religious movement?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - sects and cults
notions.definition:
**Remember** (the usual textbook meanings):
- **Sect**: a group that breaks away from a larger, older religious body and often claims that it alone has the true teaching.
- **Cult**: a group centred on a leader or special teaching, usually not a break-away; textbooks link it with secrecy and strong control of members.
- **New religious movement**: a religious group of recent origin; some mix ideas from several beliefs.

Why some people join: personal problems; hope of healing or wealth; feeling left out in their church; wish to belong.
Warnings given in textbooks: control by leaders, demands for money, family division.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: Some members leave their church, form a new group and say that only they will be saved. Is it better called a sect or a cult?
A sect. It broke away from an older religious body and claims that it alone has the truth.
notions.piege: Do not use the two words as if they meant the same. Look for the clue "breakaway", which points to a sect.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2025, Paper 1) What is a sect? Give two reasons why some people join sects.
notions.reponse: A sect is a group that has broken away from a larger religious body and follows its own interpretation of the faith. Reasons (any two): personal problems; hope of healing or wealth; feeling neglected in the mainstream church; wish to belong to a close group; strong preaching and publicity.

notions.terme: What do divination, magic, sorcery, witchcraft and superstition mean?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - african traditional religion
notions.definition:
**Remember** (textbooks differ a little):
- **Divination**: trying to find out hidden or future things through signs, objects or spirits. A **diviner** or soothsayer claims to do this.
- **Magic**: trying to control events by charms, words or special actions.
- **Sorcery**: using objects, herbs or spells, often to harm.
- **Witchcraft**: believed hidden or supernatural power, mostly linked with causing harm.
- **Superstition**: a belief without a reasonable basis, for example in omens.
- **Idolatry**: worshipping an object, image or creature as God.

These words do not describe the whole of African Traditional Religion.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: A man cancels a journey because he saw an owl and believes it brings bad luck. Name this belief.
Superstition. He takes the owl as a sign of bad luck without any reasonable proof.
notions.piege: Divination is about knowing; magic and sorcery are about making something happen.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2026, Paper 1) What is the practice of claiming to foretell the future called? What guides a man who believes that a bald head is a sign of wealth?
notions.reponse: Claiming to foretell the future is divination (soothsaying, fortune telling). The man is guided by a superstition.

notions.terme: What are the main ideas about work, trade unions, strikes and leisure?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - work and unemployment
notions.definition:
**Remember**:
- People work to earn a living, produce goods and services, develop their talents and serve others. Many believers also see work as a duty given by God.
- Workers have rights (fair and prompt pay, safe conditions, rest) and duties (honest, punctual, careful work).
- **Trade union**: workers' organisation that defends their rights and interests, first by dialogue and negotiation.
- **Strike**: workers stop work together to press their demands. It is justified when the cause is just, other means have failed, the law is respected, it is peaceful and the good expected outweighs the harm.
- **Leisure**: free time used for rest and recreation.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: Salaries are unpaid for months. Should the workers strike at once?
No. They should first talk and negotiate, for example through their trade union. If this fails, a peaceful and lawful strike can be justified, because late pay is a serious wrong.
notions.piege: A strike is not made just only by a good cause. The way it is carried out matters too: no violence and no damage to property.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2023, Paper 1) What is the main reason for trade unions? What is leisure?
notions.reponse: Trade unions exist to protect the rights and interests of workers. Leisure is free time, away from work and duties, used for rest, relaxation and recreation.

notions.terme: What are the types of justice and of peace?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - justice and human rights
notions.definition:
**Remember**: **justice** is the firm will to give each person what is due. It is one of the cardinal virtues.
- **Commutative** (contractual) justice: fairness in exchanges and contracts between persons.
- **Distributive** justice: what society owes its members; fair sharing of goods and duties.
- **Contributive** (legal) justice: what members owe society, such as paying taxes and obeying just laws.
- **Social** justice: conditions that let all people get what is due to them.

**Peace** is more than the absence of war: it needs justice. It can be inner (in the soul), family (domestic), community or social, and international.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: An employer refuses to pay the wage agreed in a contract. Which justice does he break?
Commutative justice, because he does not respect a fair exchange agreed between two parties: work for pay.
notions.piege: Check who owes what to whom. Society to citizens is distributive justice; citizens to society is contributive justice.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2025, Paper 1) What justice do citizens break when they evade taxes? What do we call the peace enjoyed in a family?
notions.reponse: They break contributive (legal) justice, what members owe to society. Peace in the family is domestic (family) peace.

notions.terme: What do incola, advena, peregrinus and vagus mean?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - homelessness and vagrancy
notions.definition:
**Remember**: these Latin words describe a person's link with a place (Catholic Church law uses them).
- **Incola**: a resident, in the place where the person has a **domicile** (permanent home).
- **Advena**: a temporary resident, where the person has a **quasi-domicile** (a home for a time).
- **Peregrinus**: a traveller or stranger, who is away from a domicile or quasi-domicile that he or she still keeps.
- **Vagus**: a person with no domicile or quasi-domicile anywhere, who wanders about.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: Mr Fon's permanent home is in Buea. He goes to Garoua for a one-week visit. What is he in Garoua?
A peregrinus. He is away from his home, but he still keeps it.
notions.piege: A peregrinus has a home somewhere else. A vagus has no home at all.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2024, Paper 1) What name is given to a person who has no home and wanders about? What is the person called who is a resident in the place of his or her permanent home?
notions.reponse: The person with no home is a vagus. The permanent resident is an incola.

notions.terme: What are the different forms of marriage?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - marriage and family
notions.definition:
**Remember**:
- **Monogamy**: one man and one woman.
- **Polygamy**: more than one spouse (general word).
- **Polygyny**: one man with several wives.
- **Polyandry**: one woman with several husbands.
- **Levirate** marriage: a man takes the widow of his dead brother.
- **Mixed** marriage: between partners of different religious backgrounds.
- **Trial** marriage: living together to test the union first.
- **Civil** marriage: before a civil status registrar. **Customary** marriage follows tradition. **Church** marriage follows Church rules.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: After the death of his brother, Ndi takes the widow as his wife, as custom demands. Name this marriage.
A levirate marriage.
notions.piege: If the question says "one man, several wives", write polygyny. Polygamy is the wider word and does not say which spouse has many partners.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2026, Paper 1) Which marriage involves only two persons? Which one joins persons of different religious backgrounds?
notions.reponse: Monogamy involves two persons. A marriage of persons of different religious backgrounds is a mixed marriage.

notions.terme: What are the types of abortion?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - sanctity of life and bioethics
notions.definition:
**Remember**: abortion is the ending of a pregnancy before the baby can live outside the womb.
- **Spontaneous** abortion (miscarriage): happens naturally; nobody intends it.
- **Induced** abortion: caused on purpose.
- **Therapeutic** abortion: done for medical reasons, for example to save the mother's life.
- **Eugenic** abortion: done because the child is expected to have a serious defect.
- **Criminal** abortion: done against the law.

Many Christians and Muslims teach that unborn life is sacred and must be protected. Views and rules differ about difficult cases.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: A pregnant woman falls ill and loses the baby, although nobody wanted this. Which type of abortion is it?
Spontaneous abortion (miscarriage), because it was not caused on purpose.
notions.piege: A therapeutic abortion is also induced. When the medical reason is given, "therapeutic" is the more exact answer.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2020, Paper 1) What is an abortion done to save the life of the pregnant woman called?

notions.terme: What are the words for acts against human life?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - sanctity of life and bioethics
notions.definition:
**Remember**:
- **Homicide**: the killing of a person. **Murder**: unlawful, intentional killing.
- **Suicide**: a person takes his or her own life.
- **Euthanasia** (mercy killing): deliberately ending the life of a suffering person to stop the suffering.
- **Genocide**: deliberate killing of many people to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
- **Mutilation**: cutting off or damaging a part of the body.

Removing a diseased part to save the whole body is justified by the principle of **totality**. Under **double effect**, a foreseen but unwanted bad effect may sometimes be accepted: the act is not wrong in itself, the aim is good, the harm is not the means, and the reason is serious.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: At a patient's request, a nurse gives an injection meant to end his life and his pain. Name the act.
Euthanasia (mercy killing). The death is intended, even though the motive is to end suffering.
notions.piege: Suicide and euthanasia differ: in suicide the person ends his or her own life; in euthanasia the usual exam meaning is that another person ends it.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2025, Paper 1) Which wrong against human life has the same person as victim and doer? Give another name for euthanasia.
notions.reponse: Suicide. Another name for euthanasia is mercy killing.

notions.terme: How do you answer "What lessons do you learn?" on a Bible or Qur'an story?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - new testament
notions.definition:
**When?** A Paper 2 question asks you to "state", "draw" or "give" lessons from a story, in any section of the paper.

**Method**
1. Read the number of lessons asked.
2. Recall what happened: who acted, what they did and what followed.
3. Choose one action or attitude to follow or to avoid.
4. Turn it into a lesson for people today: "We should ... because in the story ...".
5. Write each lesson separately, with a different idea in each one.
6. Do not retell the whole story.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: Give two lessons from Jesus' healing of the ten men with leprosy (Luke).
1. We should be grateful, because only one man came back to thank Jesus.
2. We should not despise people because of their group, because the thankful man was a Samaritan.
notions.piege: "Jesus healed ten men" is a fact from the story, not a lesson. A lesson says what we should learn or do.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2020, Paper 2) What two lessons do you learn from the conversion of Zacchaeus?
notions.reponse: Any two with a link to the story. We should repent and change our life, as Zacchaeus did. We should repay what we took wrongly: he promised to pay back four times. We should share with the poor: he gave them half of his goods. We should welcome people others reject, as Jesus did.

notions.terme: What happened at the trials of Jesus in the Gospel of Luke?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - new testament
notions.definition:
**Remember** the order (Luke 22 and 23):
1. **Jewish council** (elders, chief priests, teachers of the Law): they ask if he is the Messiah and the Son of God. They take his answer as enough to accuse him.
2. **Pilate**: they accuse him of misleading the people, opposing taxes to Caesar and claiming to be the Messiah, a king. Pilate finds no reason to condemn him. Learning that he is a Galilean, he sends him to Herod.
3. **Herod** hopes to see a miracle. Jesus does not answer. Herod and his soldiers mock him, dress him in a fine robe and send him back. Herod and Pilate become friends.
4. **Pilate** again: the crowd asks for Barabbas and for crucifixion. Pilate gives in.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: Why did Pilate send Jesus to Herod?
Pilate learnt that Jesus was a Galilean. He therefore came under the authority of Herod, who was then in Jerusalem.
notions.piege: Do not mix the trials. The question about being the Son of God belongs to the council; the hope of seeing a miracle belongs to Herod.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2024, Paper 2) Give an account of the trial of Jesus before Herod.
notions.reponse: Herod was very pleased to see Jesus, as he had heard about him and hoped to see him perform a miracle. He asked many questions, but Jesus gave no answer. The chief priests and teachers of the Law accused him strongly. Herod and his soldiers mocked him, put a fine robe on him and sent him back to Pilate. That day Herod and Pilate became friends.

notions.terme: Why is the Hadith important to Muslims, and when is it accepted as authentic?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - islamic history and hadiths
notions.definition:
**Remember**: a Hadith is a report of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did or approved. It has a chain of narrators (**isnad**) and a text (**matn**).

Importance to Muslims: it is the second source of Islamic law after the Qur'an; it explains the Qur'an; it shows how to perform acts of worship such as prayer; it guides daily conduct.

An authentic (sahih) Hadith has: an unbroken chain; honest and upright narrators; narrators with accurate memory or records; no conflict with stronger reports; no hidden defect.

Six well-known compilers: al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah. The first two rank highest.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: Why does a Muslim need the Hadith in order to pray?
Muslims learn from the Qur'an that they must pray. The Hadith shows in detail how the Prophet prayed, for example the order of the actions.
notions.piege: The isnad is the list of people who passed on the report. The matn is what the report says.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2019, Paper 2) Name the two highest-ranking compilers of Hadith and give two reasons why a Hadith may be judged authentic.
notions.reponse: Al-Bukhari and Muslim. Reasons (any two): its chain of narrators is unbroken; the narrators are upright; they preserve it accurately; it does not conflict with stronger reports; it has no hidden defect.

notions.terme: What was religious and social life like in Jahiliyya, and what did Islam reform?
notions.theme: O Level Religious Studies - islamic history and hadiths
notions.definition:
**Remember** (as taught in Islamic history): Jahiliyya, the "age of ignorance", is the period in Arabia before Islam.

Religion: worship of many idols, many kept around the Ka'ba (for example Hubal; also al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat); idols seen as a way to get nearer to God; idols honoured by bowing, going round them, sacrifices and gifts, and consulting them with arrows; fortune telling and superstition; denial by many of life after death.

Social evils: burying baby girls alive, drinking, gambling, usury, tribal wars, ill treatment of women and orphans.

Islamic reforms: worship of Allah alone; removal of idols; set prayers and a purified Hajj; belief in the Last Day; infanticide, alcohol, gambling and usury forbidden; rights for women and orphans; zakat and brotherhood.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: Match a reform to each practice: (i) idol worship, (ii) burying baby girls alive.
(i) Islam taught worship of Allah alone (tawhid), and the idols were removed from the Ka'ba.
(ii) Islam forbade the killing of children and taught that daughters have a right to life.
notions.piege: Read whether the question asks about religious life or social life, and answer only that part.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2024, Paper 2) State four bad social practices of the Jahiliyya period and the reform Islam brought to each.
notions.reponse: Any four. Baby girls buried alive: killing of children forbidden. Drinking: alcohol forbidden. Gambling: forbidden. Usury: forbidden, and charity encouraged. Tribal wars: brotherhood of believers. Women denied rights: rights given, including inheritance. Orphans cheated: their property protected.

notions.terme: How do you work out the zakat due on livestock?
notions.definition:
**When?** You are given numbers of cattle, sheep, goats or camels and a number of years.

**Method** (classical rates; animals owned for a lunar year)
1. Cattle: 1 to 29, nothing; 30 to 39, one one-year calf; 40 to 59, one two-year cow; 60 to 69, two one-year calves.
2. Larger herds: count one one-year calf for each 30, or one two-year cow for each 40.
3. Sheep or goats: 1 to 39, nothing; 40 to 120, one; 121 to 200, two; 201 to 399, three; from 400, one per full 100.
4. Camels: 1 to 4, nothing; then up to 24, one sheep or goat for each full 5.
5. Work out one year, then repeat for each year with the number then owned.
notions.exemple:
**Example**: 45 cattle, 130 goats and 12 camels are owned for one year.
45 cattle (40 to 59): one two-year cow.
130 goats (121 to 200): two goats.
12 camels (two full groups of 5): two sheep or goats.
notions.piege: Check the minimum (nisab) first: below 30 cattle, 40 sheep or goats, or 5 camels, nothing is due. Do not forget to count each year.
notions.exercice: (adapted from GCE O Level 2019, Paper 2) State the zakat on (i) 25 cattle after one year, (ii) 35 cattle after two years and (iii) 8 camels after two years. The numbers stay in the same bands.
notions.reponse:
(i) Nothing: 25 is below 30.
(ii) One one-year calf each year: two calves in all.
(iii) One sheep or goat each year: two in all.
